severities.label: Critical
severities.meaning: The flagged result cannot be relied on at all.

severities.label: Major
severities.meaning: The flagged conclusion is not supported as stated. Parts of the work may still hold.

severities.label: Caution
severities.meaning: The result may hold, but should not be relied on without the stated limitation.

severities.label: Builds on flagged work
severities.meaning: Not flagged itself, but cites work flagged Critical or Major. Computed by the build, never proposed.

categories.label: Integrity
categories.question: Is the data genuine and honestly reported?

types.label: Fabricated data
types.description: The reported data cannot have come from the study as described.
evidence: Patterns that genuine data cannot produce, shown on several values (for example repeated GRIM/SPRITE failures, or duplicated sequences or rows in shared raw data), with the calculation attached
Or an institutional or publisher finding, linked
not_enough: A single inconsistent value (use stats.impossible-values)
Results that look "too good to be true"
Digit-distribution tests such as Benford's law on their own

types.label: Altered data or results
types.description: Data or results were changed, or observations removed, without disclosure, so the reported results differ from what was observed.
evidence: Side-by-side comparison of raw or registered data with what is reported
Or an institutional or publisher finding, linked
not_enough: Disclosed exclusions the proposer disagrees with (use sample.exclusions)

types.label: Duplicated, manipulated or generated images
types.description: Figure images are duplicated, spliced, cloned, altered or generated by software (including generative models) in a way that changes what they show or presents synthetic images as observations.
evidence: Annotated image pairs or overlays with figure and panel labels
Tool name and settings, so anyone can reproduce the finding
not_enough: Compression artefacts or contrast adjustment applied to the whole image

types.label: Same data published as new
types.description: The same data or results appear in another paper, presented as new without cross-reference. Reviews and meta-analyses then count one dataset twice.
evidence: Both papers, with the matching samples, tables or results side by side

types.label: Copied data or results
types.description: Data or results were taken from another source and presented as the authors' own findings.
evidence: The original source and the copied material side by side
not_enough: Copied wording without copied data or results (out of scope)

types.label: Paper-mill product
types.description: The paper matches the template of mass-produced fraudulent papers.
evidence: Shared images, text or data with unrelated papers, listed
Or a publisher investigation, linked

types.label: Nonsense or machine-generated content
types.description: Text or analysis is generated or garbled ("tortured phrases") rather than describing real work.
evidence: Excerpts with each problem phrase and its standard term
not_enough: Suspicion of AI-assisted writing when the content is coherent and correct

types.label: False ethics, registration or data claims
types.description: The paper cites an ethics approval, trial registration or data deposit that does not exist or does not match the study.
evidence: Registry or repository lookup showing the number is absent or refers to a different study
Or a statement from the named institution

types.label: Compromised peer review
types.description: Peer review was faked or manipulated, so the paper was never independently checked.
evidence: A publisher statement, or documentary proof that reviewer identities were fake

categories.label: Evidence basis
categories.question: Is there a scientific test behind the claim at all?

types.label: No test of the claim
types.description: The claim is presented as a finding, but no data, experiment, observation or analysis in the paper tests it.
evidence: The claim, quoted
Where the methods and results were checked, and why none of them test it
not_enough: Papers labelled as essays, commentaries or hypotheses that do not present their claims as findings

types.label: Claim cannot be tested
types.description: The claim is stated so that no possible observation could count against it, yet it is presented as established.
evidence: The claim, quoted
Why no outcome would contradict it, with the paper's own wording

types.label: Anecdotes presented as general evidence
types.description: Case reports, testimonials or personal experience are used to support a general claim.
evidence: The general claim, quoted
That its support consists of individual cases or testimonials, with counts
not_enough: A case report that describes its case without generalising

types.label: Opinion or authority only
types.description: An empirical claim rests only on expert opinion, consensus or the authors' standing, with no data behind it.
evidence: The claim, quoted, and the references it relies on, shown to contain no data

categories.label: Study design
categories.question: Could this design answer the question?

types.label: Missing or unsuitable comparison
types.description: An effect is claimed without a control or comparison group, or the comparison group differs in ways that explain the result.
evidence: The effect claim, quoted
The design description showing no comparison, or the relevant difference

types.label: Obvious confounder not addressed
types.description: A factor that plausibly drives both the exposure and the outcome was not measured, adjusted for or discussed.
evidence: The confounder, with published evidence that it affects both the exposure and the outcome
That the paper neither adjusts for it nor discusses it
not_enough: A list of possible confounders without evidence that each matters

types.label: Selection on or adjustment for a common effect
types.description: The analysis selects the sample on, or adjusts for, a variable caused by both the exposure and the outcome (a collider), or adjusts for a consequence of the exposure, creating or hiding an association.
evidence: The variable and how the paper selects or adjusts on it
Why it is caused by both the exposure and the outcome (or by the exposure), with a causal diagram or published evidence
not_enough: That a different adjustment set would also be reasonable

types.label: Immortal-time or other time-related bias
types.description: Follow-up time during which the outcome could not occur in one group is counted in its favour, or exposure is defined using information from after the start of follow-up.
evidence: How the paper defines the start of follow-up and the exposure
The period that is misclassified, and why it favours one group
not_enough: That a target-trial design would have been better in general

types.label: No randomisation or blinding where the claim needs it
types.description: A causal or treatment claim is made from a design where allocation or assessment could be biased, with no randomisation or blinding.
evidence: The claim, and the allocation and assessment procedure as described

types.label: Measure does not capture the claim
types.description: The instrument, proxy or outcome measure does not measure what the conclusion is about, or has not been validated for this use.
evidence: The measure and the claim side by side
Validation literature, or its absence, for this population and use

types.label: Misidentified or contaminated materials
types.description: Cell lines, organisms, reagents or antibodies were not what the paper says they were.
evidence: A register entry (for example ICLAC or Cellosaurus) or authentication data

types.label: Instrument or measurement artefact
types.description: The result is produced by equipment fault, calibration error or a known artefact of the method.
evidence: The artefact demonstrated, or documented for this instrument or method

types.label: Wrong timescale or dose for the claim
types.description: Follow-up, exposure or dose is too short or too small for the claimed effect to appear or be ruled out.
evidence: The claim, and published evidence on the timescale or dose it needs

types.label: Unvalidated model presented as a finding
types.description: Results come from a model or simulation whose key assumptions were not tested, and are presented as empirical findings.
evidence: The assumptions that drive the result, and why they are untested
Ideally, the result changing under a reasonable alternative assumption

categories.label: Sample
categories.question: Who or what was studied, and was it enough?

types.label: Sample too small for the claim
types.description: The sample cannot reliably detect or estimate the effect claimed.
evidence: A power or precision calculation (for example confidence interval width) using the paper's own numbers
not_enough: A claim that the sample "seems small", with no calculation

types.label: Sample does not match the claim
types.description: The claim covers a population that the sample does not represent (convenience, single site, WEIRD, one sex or age group).
evidence: The generalising claim, quoted, and the sample description

types.label: Selection bias
types.description: Who ended up in the sample depends on the outcome or on factors linked to it (self-selection, survivorship, selecting on the outcome).
evidence: The recruitment or inclusion route, and how it links to the outcome

types.label: Dropout or missing data not handled
types.description: High or unequal dropout or missing data could explain the result, and the analysis does not deal with it.
evidence: Numbers enrolled and analysed per group, and the handling described

types.label: Undisclosed or after-the-fact exclusions
types.description: Participants or data points were excluded without reporting, or by rules set after seeing results.
evidence: Numbers that do not add up between stages, or rules that differ from the registration

categories.label: Numbers and statistics
categories.question: Are the numbers and analyses right?

types.label: Impossible or inconsistent numbers
types.description: Reported values cannot all be true: means impossible for the sample size, p-values that do not match test statistics, totals that do not add up.
evidence: Each inconsistent value, with the recalculation
Whether the inconsistency affects the conclusion (sets severity)

types.label: Wrong test or broken assumptions
types.description: The statistical method does not fit the data or design, and using the right one changes the conclusion.
evidence: Why the method does not fit
The result with a suitable method, or why it cannot be computed from what is reported

types.label: Pseudoreplication
types.description: Repeated measurements of the same unit are treated as independent, inflating the sample size.
evidence: The true independent units and the n used in the analysis

types.label: Selective analysis (p-hacking)
types.description: Several analyses were evidently tried and the favourable ones reported, without disclosure.
evidence: Undisclosed analytic choices shown against a registration, earlier version or the paper's own data
Or a clustering of key p-values just under the threshold across the paper, with the list
not_enough: A single p-value near the threshold

types.label: Many tests, no correction
types.description: Many comparisons were run and the significant few reported as findings, without correction or acknowledgement.
evidence: The number of tests run and which results survive correction

types.label: Outcome switched from registration
types.description: The primary outcome or hypothesis in the paper differs from the registration, without disclosure.
evidence: Registry snapshot and paper side by side, with dates

types.label: Outcomes measured but not reported
types.description: Outcomes the protocol, registration or methods say were measured are missing from the results, with no explanation.
evidence: The protocol, registration or methods section listing the outcome
That the results and supplements do not report it
not_enough: Outcomes the reader would have liked that were never planned

types.label: Meta-analysis counts or extracts wrongly
types.description: A meta-analysis counts the same participants or study twice, takes effect sizes or variances from the wrong place, mixes incompatible measures, or includes studies its own criteria exclude.
evidence: The included studies concerned, with the numbers the meta-analysis used and the numbers in the source
The pooled estimate recomputed without the error, where possible
not_enough: Disagreement with the inclusion criteria themselves

types.label: After-the-fact hypothesis presented as planned
types.description: A hypothesis formed after seeing results is presented as tested in advance.
evidence: An earlier version, preprint or registration with a different hypothesis

types.label: Circular analysis or data leakage
types.description: The same data select and test the effect, or test data leak into training, so the result is built in.
evidence: The step where selection and testing share data, or where leakage occurs

types.label: "No significant difference" read as "no effect"
types.description: A non-significant result is presented as showing that there is no effect or that groups are equal.
evidence: The claim, and the confidence interval showing meaningful effects remain possible

types.label: Misleading effect size
types.description: The effect is presented in a way that misleads about its size, such as relative risk without absolute risk.
evidence: The presented figure and the plain figure from the same data

types.label: Aggregation error
types.description: A group-level pattern is claimed for individuals, or a pattern reverses when the data are split or combined (ecological fallacy, Simpson's paradox).
evidence: The level of the data and the level of the claim, or the reversed pattern shown

types.label: Regression to the mean read as an effect
types.description: Units selected for extreme values are re-measured, and their natural drift back is presented as an effect.
evidence: The selection on extreme values and the absence of a comparison group

types.label: Calculation or code error
types.description: A specific error in calculation or analysis code changes the reported results.
evidence: The error located in the authors' code or calculation, and the corrected result

categories.label: Reasoning and conclusions
categories.question: Do the conclusions follow from the results?

types.label: Conclusion goes beyond the results
types.description: The abstract or conclusion claims more than the results show.
evidence: The conclusion and the relevant result side by side

types.label: Title or abstract reports a different result
types.description: The title or abstract presents a secondary, subgroup or within-group finding as the main result, or leaves out a primary result that did not support the hypothesis.
evidence: The title or abstract and the primary result in the paper, side by side
not_enough: Wording that is enthusiastic but matches the results

types.label: Overgeneralisation
types.description: Results are extended beyond the population, species, setting or conditions studied (for example mice to humans) without evidence.
evidence: The generalising claim and the conditions actually studied

types.label: Cause claimed from correlation
types.description: A causal conclusion is drawn from a design that can show only association.
evidence: The causal wording, quoted, and the design

types.label: Paper contradicts itself
types.description: The abstract, text, tables or figures state incompatible things.
evidence: The contradicting passages, quoted with locations

types.label: Invalid argument
types.description: The conclusion does not follow logically from its premises (circular reasoning, false dichotomy, affirming the consequent).
evidence: Premises and conclusion, quoted, and where the logic breaks

types.label: Error in derivation or proof
types.description: A mathematical or theoretical derivation contains an error that the result depends on.
evidence: The faulty step, and a counterexample or the corrected derivation

types.label: Ignores directly contrary evidence
types.description: The paper claims novelty or consensus while omitting earlier published work that directly tested the same question with a different result.
evidence: The earlier work, published before submission, on the same question
not_enough: Work the proposer finds relevant that does not test the same question

categories.label: Sources and citations
categories.question: Does it rest on sound, correctly cited work?

types.label: Source does not say what is claimed
types.description: A cited source is used for a claim it does not make, so the error enters the literature under the source's authority.
evidence: The citing sentence, and the relevant passages of the cited source

types.label: Key claim rests on flagged work
types.description: A key claim depends on work that is retracted or flagged Critical or Major. Citing flagged work in passing does not qualify.
evidence: The key claim, and how it depends on the flagged work

types.label: Reference does not exist
types.description: Cited works cannot be found and appear not to exist.
evidence: Each reference, with the failed lookups (DOI, catalogue, publisher)

types.label: Key claim rests on an unreliable source
types.description: A key claim relies on a withdrawn preprint, a hijacked journal or another source without genuine review, presented as established.
evidence: The claim, the source, and documentation of the source's status

types.label: Irrelevant citations
types.description: Many citations are unrelated to the content, as seen in citation cartels and coercive citation.
evidence: Each irrelevant citation, and why it is unrelated to the citing text

categories.label: Transparency and reproducibility
categories.question: Can others check and repeat it?

types.label: Failed replication
types.description: Independent, adequately powered replications following the original method did not find the result.
evidence: The replication(s), linked, with their power and protocol
not_enough: One underpowered replication, or one with a different method

types.label: Results not reproduced from the same data
types.description: Re-running the reported analysis on the authors' own data does not give the reported results.
evidence: The data and code used, and the differing results

types.label: Result depends on arbitrary choices
types.description: The result disappears under reasonable alternative analysis choices.
evidence: The alternatives run, and why each is as reasonable as the original

types.label: Data or code unavailable
types.description: Data or code the paper says are available are not, or were refused on request for a key claim.
evidence: The availability statement, and dated requests or failed links (names removed)
rw_reasons: Original Data and/or Images not Provided and/or not Available

types.label: Methods too vague to repeat
types.description: The methods lack details needed to repeat the study.
evidence: The missing details, listed

categories.label: Conflicts of interest
categories.question: Who had a stake, and was it disclosed?
categories.note: A conflict of interest does not make a result wrong. It raises the risk, so these flags are Caution unless the interested party controlled the work.

types.label: Undisclosed financial interest
types.description: Authors had funding, employment, equity, patents or payments linked to the result and did not disclose them.
evidence: Documentary proof (funding records, patents, company filings, disclosures in other papers of the same period)
The paper's own disclosure statement

types.label: Undisclosed non-financial interest
types.description: Authors evaluated their own product or method, or held a documented formal role tied to the outcome, and did not disclose it.
evidence: Documentary proof of the role or ownership, and the disclosure statement
not_enough: Inferred beliefs, politics or personal views

types.label: Funder controlled the study
types.description: A party with a stake in the result controlled the design, analysis or decision to publish.
evidence: A contract, protocol, correspondence or official statement showing the control

categories.label: Official notices
categories.question: What have the journal or publisher said?

types.label: Retracted
types.description: The paper has been retracted. A retraction whose only reasons do not concern the validity of the work (retract-and-replace, a publisher's error, withdrawal to publish elsewhere) is Caution.
evidence: The retraction notice

types.label: Expression of concern
types.description: The publisher has formally questioned the paper's reliability.
evidence: The notice

types.label: Correction affecting conclusions
types.description: A published correction changes results or conclusions.
evidence: The correction
and what it changes

types.label: Withdrawn preprint
types.description: The authors or server withdrew the preprint.
evidence: The withdrawal notice

outOfScope: Motives, politics or ideology of authors. Only their visible effects on the work are flaggable.
Disagreeing with consensus, novelty or unpopular conclusions. Contradicting accepted views is not an error.
People. Flags attach to papers and claims, never to authors, labs or institutions.
Writing quality, typos and copied wording without copied data or results.
Ethics violations that do not affect validity. These belong with the institution or journal.
